question: In the lecture, the norm of a partition is defined as the length of the longest subinterval. Explain why this definition is used and how it affects the construction of the Riemann sum for a continuous function \(f\) on \([A,B]\) when the tags are chosen to be the right endpoints of the subintervals.
answer: The norm \(\|P\|\) of a partition \(P\) measures how fine the partition is; it is the maximum length of the subintervals \([x_{i-1},x_i]\). Using the norm ensures that as \(\|P\|\to 0\) the mesh of the partition becomes arbitrarily small, which is necessary for the Riemann sums to approximate the integral of a continuous function. When the tags are taken to be the right endpoints \(x_i\), each term of the Riemann sum is \(f(x_i)\,\Delta x_i\) where \(\Delta x_i=x_i-x_{i-1}\). Because \(f\) is continuous, the value of \(f\) on each subinterval is well approximated by its value at the right endpoint when the subinterval is small. Thus, as the norm decreases, the Riemann sums with right‑endpoint tags converge to the true area under \(f\) on \([A,B]\).

question: In the lecture, why is the norm of a partition important for the convergence of Riemann sums of a continuous function, and how does the choice of tags (for example, using right endpoints) affect the Riemann sum while leaving the limit unchanged?
answer: The norm of a partition, denoted \(\|P\|\), is the length of the longest subinterval in the partition. As \(\|P\|\) tends to zero, the mesh of the partition becomes finer, and for a continuous function \(f\) the values of \(f\) at any point in a subinterval become arbitrarily close to the value at the chosen tag. This ensures that the Riemann sum \(S(P,f)=\sum f(t_i)\,\Delta x_i\) approximates the integral more accurately. The specific choice of tags (right endpoints, left endpoints, or any point in each subinterval) only changes the individual terms of the sum, but for a continuous function the difference between any two such sums tends to zero as \(\|P\|\to0\). Consequently, all Riemann sums converge to the same limit, the Riemann integral of \(f\).
